page_checks.summary: Distinguishes determinative-level and noun-phrase-level modification, including not, approximation, and degree.
Completeness modifiers and than-complements accompany upper and lower bounds. The footnotes qualify numeral placement and the structure of no more.
Post-head PP modifiers can be delayed. Range PPs and four subtypes of predeterminers are introduced.
All before a numeral differs from all before a definite determiner. Fraction and multiplier constructions have distinct distribution and partitive alternatives.
Such and exclamative what contrast with degree AdjPs and analytic comparatives. The legal register has a separate determinative such.
Some predeterminers stack. Passive placement distinguishes clause and NP scope for peripheral modifiers, with focusing examples.
Reinforcement, approximation, negative approximation, negation, and precision show construction-specific peripheral placement.
Frequency, domain, modal, evaluative, predicative quantification, reflexives, and layered combinations illustrate peripheral modification.
Internal nominal dependents are organized by position and function. Nominal, adjectival, PP, and clause complements are distinguished.
Complements depend on head-noun licensing. Optionality and the prepositions taken by deverbal nouns vary.
Anaphoric one gives limited evidence of complement status, while attributive complement adjacency is stricter than post-head ordering.
Of-complements encode several semantic relations. The evaluative predicand construction and lack of nominal dummy or raised complements are discussed.
Semantic roles depend on the head. Indirect complements are licensed by other dependents, with limits on relocation.
Attributive modifiers come from several categories but usually exclude their own post-head dependents. Nonce formations are separate.
Comparative determinatives and enough have restricted postpositive uses. Adjective placement depends on structure and lexical sense.
Post-head modifiers include restricted NPs, PPs, and relative or nonfinite clauses. Stacking is supported by coordination and anaphora.
Stacking differs from submodification and multiple complements. Integrated appositives show systematic entailments without always being restrictive.
Content clauses are complements. Of-marked appositives permit proper-name obliques, and the composite nominal distinction is introduced.
Independent coordination and modification distinguish composite nominals from compound bases, with limits on separately modifying the head.
Transparent compounds can fail the syntactic tests. Context-driven reanalysis explains some borderline coordination.
Stress, spelling, specialized meaning, and productivity do not reliably replace syntactic evidence.
Rigid ordering constraints differ from labile defaults. The noun phrase ordering template and external modifier sequence are given.
Early modifiers can change order and scope. Residual modifier ordering is described as a semantic preference.
Provenance, manufacture, and type complete the residual inventory. Weight affects post-head order, with specialized rigid restrictions.
